subject: Religionskunskap 1
title: The world religions: a comparative study
sourceSummary: A comparative study of how Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism view God and the afterlife, and of the internal diversity of denominations and interpretive traditions within each religion.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between the conception of God within monotheistic religions (Judaism, Christianity, Islam) and Hinduism?
questions.opener: Hinduism is usually described as more multifaceted in its conception of God than the three Abrahamic religions.
choices: Monotheistic religions believe in a single god, while Hinduism contains a great diversity of conceptions of God, from the worship of many gods (seen as expressions of an underlying reality, Brahman) to more philosophical, impersonal conceptions of God
All five religions have exactly the same conception of God
Hinduism has no conceptions of divinity at all
Judaism, Christianity and Islam have completely different gods with no common root
questions.explanation: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are counted as monotheistic and share a common Abrahamic root in the conception of a single God, albeit with different understandings of God's nature. Hinduism is more multifaceted: many Hindus worship several gods as different expressions of an underlying reality (Brahman), while other currents emphasise a more philosophical, impersonal conception of God — there is thus no single "Hindu conception of God".

questions.prompt: How does the conception of God within Buddhism generally differ from the Abrahamic religions?
questions.opener: Consider what role a creator god plays in Buddhism's teaching on suffering and liberation.
choices: Buddhism places a creator god at the centre in the same way Islam does

Traditional Buddhism does not focus on a creator god, but on insight, mindful presence and liberation from suffering (nirvana); the question of the existence of gods is often given subordinate importance
Buddhists actively deny that any gods have ever been mentioned in Buddhist texts
Buddhism and Islam have an identical conception of God
questions.explanation: Buddhism has not historically centred on an almighty creator god in the way Judaism, Christianity and Islam do; the focus instead lies on insight into the nature of existence and liberation from suffering. Divine beings appear in some Buddhist traditions and texts, but do not play the same central, decisive role as in the monotheistic religions.

questions.prompt: What characterises the view of the afterlife within Hinduism and Buddhism, compared with the Abrahamic religions?
questions.opener: Consider the concepts of rebirth and karma, which are central to both Asian traditions.
choices: All religions share exactly the same view of an eternal life in paradise or hell

Hinduism and Buddhism are often associated with conceptions of rebirth (samsara), in which karma affects the next life, while Judaism, Christianity and Islam more often emphasise a final state after death, such as eternal life or resurrection
Hinduism and Buddhism have no conceptions at all of what happens after death
The Abrahamic religions all believe in rebirth
questions.explanation: Within Hinduism and Buddhism, the conception of samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth shaped by karma, is central, even though the goal (moksha and nirvana respectively) is ultimately to break the cycle. The Abrahamic religions instead usually emphasise a final state after death, such as paradise, resurrection or judgement, rather than repeated rebirth — although views vary between and within the traditions.

questions.prompt: Which statement best holds true about internal diversity within Islam?
questions.opener: Consider whether all Muslims worldwide interpret their faith and practice in exactly the same way.
choices: Islam has no internal diversity at all, all Muslims believe and practise identically
Islam contains several denominations, above all Sunni and Shia, as well as different schools of law and spiritual traditions such as Sufism, which can differ in interpretation, practice and emphasis
Only Sunni Islam counts as "real" Islam from a religious studies point of view
Shia and Sunni Muslims believe in entirely different gods
questions.explanation: Like other world religions, Islam contains considerable internal diversity, with Sunni and Shia as the largest denominations, different schools of law (madhhab) and spiritual traditions such as Sufism. Religious studies describes this diversity neutrally, without ranking which denomination is "most correct".

questions.prompt: Why can two people within the same religion, both proceeding from the same sacred text, nonetheless arrive at different conclusions about how one should live?
questions.opener: Consider that a text rarely "speaks for itself" but is interpreted in light of tradition, context and interpretive principles.
choices: It is impossible, a sacred text can only be interpreted in a single way

Sacred texts are often interpreted in light of different interpretive traditions, historical context and authorities, which means the same text can give rise to differing practices and teachings within one and the same religion
In that case, only one of the people can count as truly religious
Interpretation of sacred texts only occurs within Christianity
questions.explanation: Interpretation (exegesis) of sacred texts always takes place within a tradition, with the help of commentaries, authorities and methods developed over time, which means differing interpretive traditions can arrive at different conclusions from the same base text. This phenomenon exists within all world religions built on written texts, not just Christianity.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of religion and central sacred scripture is correct?
questions.opener: Match the religion with the text traditionally regarded as its foremost scripture.
choices: Judaism – the Torah, Islam – the Qur'an, Hinduism – the Vedas
Buddhism – the Qur'an, Judaism – the Bhagavad Gita
Islam – the Torah, Christianity – the Vedas
Hinduism – the Bible, Judaism – the Qur'an
questions.explanation: The Torah is Judaism's central scripture, the Qur'an is regarded within Islam as God's revealed word to the prophet Muhammad, and the Vedas are among Hinduism's oldest and most authoritative texts. The other options mix up religions and scriptures that do not belong together in that way.

questions.prompt: Compare the view of the afterlife within Christianity and Buddhism. What similarities and differences are there, and what do the differences stem from?
questions.opener: Start from the key concepts: resurrection/eternal life for Christianity, samsara/nirvana for Buddhism.
questions.answer: Within Christianity, one generally believes in an eternal life after death, often linked to Jesus' resurrection and a final judgement, in which the soul (or the whole person, depending on denomination) is either united with God or separated from God. Life is usually seen as a single, decisive passage leading up to this final state. Within Buddhism, the starting point is instead samsara, a cyclical process of birth, death and rebirth shaped by karma, and the goal is to reach nirvana through insight and ethical training, a state beyond suffering and craving, rather than a place like paradise. One similarity is that both traditions link what happens after death to how one has lived: deeds and disposition matter in both systems. An important difference is the structure of time: Christianity generally envisages a single life followed by an eternal state, while Buddhism proceeds from repeated lives until liberation is attained. The differences are connected to different underlying worldviews: a creator god and a linear conception of time in Christianity, compared with a cyclical conception of time and a focus on cause and effect (karma) in Buddhism.
steps: Describe the Christian conception: eternal life after death, linked to resurrection and a final relationship with God.
Describe the Buddhist conception: samsara (the cycle of rebirth) shaped by karma, with nirvana as the ultimate goal.
Identify a similarity: in both traditions, the life lived (deeds, disposition) affects what happens after death.
Identify a difference: linear time and a single decisive life in Christianity, compared with cyclical time and repeated lives in Buddhism.
Link the difference to an underlying cause: different fundamental worldviews about time, divinity and causation.

questions.prompt: Summarise conceptions of God, conceptions of the afterlife, internal diversity and sacred texts in the five major world religions.
questions.opener: Go through the conception of God, the afterlife, internal diversity and sacred texts in turn.
questions.answer: Conceptions of God: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are monotheistic (one God) · Hinduism contains everything from the worship of many gods to a philosophical, impersonal conception of God (Brahman) · Buddhism does not primarily focus on a creator god, but on insight and liberation. Afterlife: Judaism/Christianity/Islam often emphasise a final state (resurrection, eternal life, judgement) · Hinduism/Buddhism proceed from samsara (rebirth shaped by karma) with moksha and nirvana respectively as the goal. Internal diversity: every religion contains several denominations, e.g. Sunni/Shia within Islam, Catholicism/Protestantism/Orthodoxy within Christianity, various schools within Hinduism and Buddhism. Sacred texts: the Torah (Judaism), the Bible (Christianity), the Qur'an (Islam), the Vedas (Hinduism) and Buddhist canonical texts · the same text can be interpreted differently within a tradition depending on interpretive tradition and context.
